_note: Extensive explainers for every freight route on the dashboard. Route codes like TD3C are industry shorthand and mean nothing to a newcomer, so each one is clickable wherever it appears — in the rate table, in the brief, and in headlines. Keyed by the dashboard's row id; `code` is what the market calls it.

routes.name: Middle East Gulf to China
routes.vessel: VLCC — Very Large Crude Carrier, around 300,000 dwt
routes.cargo: 270,000 tonnes of crude oil, roughly 2 million barrels
routes.voyage: Loads at a Gulf terminal such as Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia and discharges in China, typically Ningbo. About 6,000 nautical miles each way; a full round trip including the empty return takes roughly 40 to 45 days.
routes.quoted: Agreed in Worldscale points, then converted to a round-trip TCE in dollars per day. The TCE is the figure that tells you whether the owner is making money, because it subtracts fuel and port costs and counts the ballast leg home.
routes.why: The single most quoted tanker rate in the world. When a broker or an analyst says 'VLCC earnings', they almost always mean this route. It is the benchmark because it is the largest, longest and most liquid crude trade there is.
moves: Chinese crude buying, which sets how many cargoes are looking for ships
OPEC+ production decisions, since fewer barrels means fewer fixtures
Anything affecting the Strait of Hormuz, the only way out of the Gulf
Bunker prices, which come straight off the TCE
Floating storage, which removes ships from the trading fleet
routes.watch: A high Worldscale number does not automatically mean high earnings. The Worldscale flat rate resets every January, and fuel costs are deducted from the owner's side, so always look at the TCE rather than the WS figure.

routes.name: West Africa to UK Continent
routes.vessel: Suezmax — around 150,000 dwt, sized to transit the Suez Canal fully laden
routes.cargo: 130,000 tonnes of crude oil, roughly 1 million barrels
routes.voyage: Loads in Nigeria, usually Bonny, and discharges in northwest Europe. About 4,000 nautical miles each way, with a round trip of roughly 30 days.
routes.quoted: Worldscale points converted to a round-trip TCE in dollars per day.
routes.why: The benchmark for the mid-size crude fleet and for the Atlantic basin. Suezmaxes are the flexible middle of the crude market: too big for many regional trades, too small for the Gulf-to-Asia run, so they pick up whatever the pattern of trade creates.
moves: Nigerian and Angolan production and export programmes
European refinery demand for light sweet crude
VLCC rates, because when the biggest ships get expensive charterers split cargoes into Suezmaxes instead
Rerouting away from the Suez Canal, which lengthens voyages
routes.watch: Suezmax rates often follow VLCC rates with a short delay rather than moving independently. If you see VLCCs spike, expect this to follow.

routes.name: North Sea to UK Continent
routes.voyage: Loads at Hound Point in Scotland and discharges at Wilhelmshaven in Germany. Only about 400 nautical miles, so a round trip is a matter of days rather than weeks.
routes.quoted: Worldscale points converted to a round-trip TCE, quoted basis Hound Point to Wilhelmshaven — meaning those exact ports are the assumption behind the number.
routes.why: This is the North Sea crude route, which makes it the single most relevant tanker rate to Norwegian oil exports. Short-haul routes behave differently from long-haul ones: with so few days at sea, a day of delay or a day of waiting changes the daily earnings dramatically, so rates here are unusually volatile.
moves: North Sea loading programmes, including Norwegian fields
Weather in the North Sea, which delays loading and tightens tonnage
Refinery demand and maintenance in northwest Europe
Baltic and Mediterranean Aframax demand, since the ships compete for the same cargoes
routes.watch: Because the voyage is so short, the daily TCE on this route swings far more than on a long-haul run. A single idle day is a much larger share of the voyage.

routes.name: Middle East Gulf to Japan
routes.vessel: LR2 — Long Range 2, around 110,000 dwt. The same hull as an Aframax, but with coated tanks so it can carry clean cargoes.
routes.cargo: 75,000 tonnes of clean petroleum products, typically naphtha
routes.voyage: Loads at a Gulf refinery and discharges in Japan, about 6,500 nautical miles each way.
routes.quoted: Worldscale points converted to a round-trip TCE in dollars per day.
routes.why: The benchmark for large product tankers east of Suez. It matters because an LR2 can switch between clean products and crude depending on which pays better, which links the clean and dirty tanker markets together.
moves: Middle East refinery output, especially new export refineries
Asian naphtha demand from petrochemical plants
Refining margins, since fat margins make refineries run harder and produce more cargo
The crude market, because when crude rates are strong LR2s switch across and tighten clean supply
routes.watch: When LR2s move into crude trades, the clean product fleet effectively shrinks. Watching that switch is one of the more useful things to follow in tankers.

routes.name: Rotterdam to New York
routes.cargo: 37,000 tonnes of clean products, classically gasoline
routes.voyage: Loads in the Amsterdam–Rotterdam–Antwerp area and discharges on the US Atlantic coast. About 3,300 nautical miles each way.
routes.quoted: Worldscale points converted to a round-trip TCE in dollars per day.
routes.why: The classic transatlantic gasoline route and the most watched MR benchmark. Europe produces surplus gasoline it does not consume; the US east coast consumes more than it refines. That structural mismatch is what keeps this trade alive.
moves: US gasoline inventories and the American driving season
European refinery runs and maintenance
The gasoline arbitrage — whether US prices exceed European prices by more than the cost of shipping
Hurricanes on the US Gulf coast, which disrupt refining and reshape flows
routes.watch: This route is seasonal in a way most are not. Demand builds ahead of the US summer driving season and fades afterwards.

routes.name: US Gulf to UK Continent
routes.voyage: Loads on the US Gulf coast and discharges in northwest Europe, about 4,700 nautical miles each way.
routes.quoted: Worldscale points converted to a round-trip TCE in dollars per day.
routes.why: The eastbound counterpart to TC2. Together the two describe the transatlantic product triangle: ships carry gasoline west, then look for a cargo to bring back east rather than sailing empty.
moves: US refinery output on the Gulf coast
European diesel demand, particularly in winter
Whether owners can link a westbound and an eastbound cargo, which decides how many ballast days they eat
routes.watch: Compare this with TC2. When one leg pays far better than the other, owners reposition, and the weaker leg eventually tightens.

routes.name: Capesize five-route average
routes.vessel: Capesize — around 180,000 dwt. Too large for the Suez and Panama canals, hence the name: historically it sailed around the Cape of Good Hope.
routes.cargo: Iron ore and coal, in cargoes of roughly 150,000 to 180,000 tonnes
routes.voyage: An average across five benchmark routes rather than a single voyage, covering the main iron ore and coal trades — principally Australia and Brazil to China.
routes.quoted: Directly in dollars per day, as an average of the five time charter routes. No Worldscale conversion is involved, which makes dry bulk rates easier to read than tanker rates.
routes.why: The headline earnings figure for the largest bulk carriers, and the heaviest component of the Baltic Dry Index. When owners describe what their Capesizes are earning, this is the number they quote.
moves: Chinese steel production, which drives iron ore imports
Whether China buys from Brazil or Australia — Brazil is far further, so the same tonnage creates far more tonne-miles
Coal demand, which rises when gas prices make coal-fired power cheaper
Port congestion and weather at loading terminals
The orderbook, since a wave of deliveries caps rates years ahead
routes.watch: Capesize earnings are the most volatile in dry bulk and can double or halve within weeks. They are effectively a bet on Chinese steel.

routes.name: Panamax four-route average
routes.vessel: Panamax or Kamsarmax — around 82,000 dwt, sized to fit the Panama Canal locks
routes.cargo: Coal and grain, in cargoes of roughly 60,000 to 80,000 tonnes
routes.voyage: An average across four benchmark time charter routes.
routes.quoted: Dollars per day, averaged across the four routes.
routes.why: The mid-size dry bulk benchmark. Panamaxes carry the cargoes that feed power stations and people rather than steel mills, so they follow a different rhythm from Capesizes.
moves: Grain harvests in North and South America, which are genuinely seasonal
Coal imports for power generation, which rise with gas prices and cold weather
Panama Canal transit availability, which drought has restricted in recent years
routes.watch: This is the most seasonal dry bulk segment. North American grain exports peak late in the year and South American exports peak in spring.

routes.name: Supramax ten-route average
routes.vessel: Supramax or Ultramax — around 58,000 dwt, fitted with its own cranes
routes.cargo: Minor bulks: cement, fertiliser, steel products, bauxite, sugar, salt
routes.voyage: An average across ten benchmark routes, spread across more regions than the larger classes.
routes.quoted: Dollars per day, averaged across the ten routes.
routes.why: The most flexible dry bulk class. Because these ships carry their own cranes, they can work ports with no shore equipment, which opens up trades the bigger ships cannot touch.
moves: Broad global trade rather than any single commodity
Construction and infrastructure activity, which drives cement and steel movements
Regional disruptions, since these ships serve many small ports
routes.watch: Because its cargoes are spread across many commodities and regions, this is usually the steadiest dry bulk segment. That makes it a better read on general trade than the Capesize market.

routes.name: Handysize seven-route average
routes.vessel: Handysize — around 38,000 dwt, geared, the smallest Baltic-assessed bulker
routes.cargo: Minor bulks, in smaller parcels and to smaller ports
routes.voyage: An average across seven benchmark routes.
routes.quoted: Dollars per day, averaged across the seven routes.
routes.why: The small end of dry bulk. These ships reach shallow and underdeveloped ports that nothing larger can enter, so they serve trades the rest of the fleet cannot.
moves: Regional agricultural and construction demand
Access to smaller ports, where draft and crane availability matter
The broad dry bulk cycle, though with less violent swings than Capesize
routes.watch: Handysize rates are the least tied to iron ore and China of any dry bulk class, which makes them a useful cross-check when the BDI is being driven by one commodity.

routes.name: Australia to Japan
routes.vessel: LNG carrier of about 160,000 cubic metres, modern two-stroke propulsion
routes.cargo: Liquefied natural gas — gas chilled to about minus 162°C, which shrinks it roughly 600 times so it can be shipped
routes.voyage: Loads at an Australian liquefaction plant and discharges in Japan. About 3,500 nautical miles — short, by LNG standards.
routes.quoted: Directly in dollars per day for a spot charter.
routes.why: The Pacific basin benchmark. Australia and Qatar are the traditional suppliers to North Asia, and this is the short-haul route that sets the floor for Pacific LNG shipping.
moves: Japanese and Korean winter heating demand
Nuclear restarts in Japan, which reduce the need for imported gas
The gap between Asian and European gas prices, which decides where cargoes sail
Availability of ships in the Pacific basin
routes.watch: Compare this with BLNG3. If the US-to-Japan route pays far more, ships reposition towards the Atlantic and Pacific supply tightens.

routes.name: US Gulf to Continent
routes.vessel: LNG carrier of about 160,000 cubic metres
routes.voyage: Loads at a US Gulf export terminal such as Sabine Pass and discharges in northwest Europe. About 4,800 nautical miles.
routes.quoted: Dollars per day for a spot charter.
routes.why: The Atlantic benchmark, and the short leg of the US export trade. US LNG exports are the fastest-growing part of the market, and this is the route they take when Europe is paying more than Asia.
moves: European gas prices, especially TTF, and how full European storage is
US liquefaction plant output and any outages
The TTF to JKM spread, which decides whether a cargo turns left to Europe or right to Asia
routes.watch: The difference between this and BLNG3 is one of the clearest examples in shipping of price gaps creating freight demand. Same ship, same cargo, two very different voyage lengths.

routes.name: US Gulf to Japan
routes.vessel: LNG carrier of about 160,000 cubic metres
routes.voyage: Loads on the US Gulf coast and discharges in Japan, either through the Panama Canal or the long way round. Roughly 9,000 nautical miles via Panama and considerably further if the canal is unavailable.
routes.quoted: Dollars per day for a spot charter.
routes.why: The long-haul LNG benchmark. It pays the most of the three because the voyage ties a ship up for far longer, and it is the clearest measure of how much work the LNG fleet is being asked to do.
moves: The gap between Asian JKM and European TTF prices
Panama Canal transit availability, since a closed canal adds weeks
Asian winter demand
US export volumes
routes.watch: This is where tonne-miles show up most clearly. The same cargo sailing to Japan instead of Europe roughly doubles the work, which is why LNG shipping can tighten without a single extra tonne being produced.

routes.name: Ras Tanura to Chiba
routes.vessel: VLGC — Very Large Gas Carrier, about 84,000 cubic metres
routes.cargo: LPG — propane and butane, shipped as a liquid under pressure
routes.voyage: Loads at Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia and discharges at Chiba in Japan, roughly 6,500 nautical miles.
routes.quoted: Quoted in dollars per tonne of cargo, and then converted to a TCE in dollars per day — so you will see both figures in the same sentence.
routes.why: The benchmark for the long-haul LPG trade. LPG is a by-product of gas processing and oil refining, so this market is driven by production elsewhere rather than by demand for LPG itself.
moves: US and Middle East LPG export volumes
The propane price gap between the US, Europe and Asia
Panama Canal delays, which hit the competing US-to-Asia route and push cargoes onto Gulf loadings
Asian petrochemical demand, where propane competes with naphtha as a feedstock
routes.watch: Watch the dollars-per-tonne figure and the dollars-per-day figure separately. A rate per tonne can fall while daily earnings hold up, if the voyage gets shorter or faster.
